edge.title: The scheme that always pays on time
edge.setup: A neighbour or relative shows you the payouts: interest credited on the dot every month, a bond certificate, a friendly local agent who earns a commission for bringing you in. The return is a few points above anything a bank or mutual fund offers, and it is described as safe because it is 'asset-backed' or 'land-backed'.
edge.tell: A return that is higher than the market and also guaranteed, paid out to you by recruiting more people like you.
move: Ask who regulates it. A deposit or investment scheme should be traceable to a registered regulator such as SEBI or RBI, or be a bank product; a certificate alone proves nothing.
Do not judge it by the payouts you have seen. Early payouts are what the scheme spends to look real.
If money is already in, stop adding more and do not recruit anyone. Report to the police or the state CID economic offences unit and keep every receipt and bond.
edge.why: Guaranteed high returns cannot be earned honestly, so the money paying old investors can only be coming from new investors. The people you meet are the ones who were paid, so the evidence always looks good, and agents who earn commission believe it too. It collapses when new money slows, and by then the people still inside hold the loss.
edge.variants: Same shape: chit-fund and 'land bond' schemes, crypto or forex 'doubling' groups, multi-level marketing where the real product is the next recruit.

scenario.question: A relative shows you a scheme that has paid them 2% a month, on time, for a year. The local agent offers you the same, says it is backed by land, hands you a printed bond certificate, and adds that you get a bonus for each person you bring in. What do you do?

choices.text: Ask which regulator it is registered with, such as SEBI or RBI, and check that yourself. If you cannot trace it to one, put nothing in and bring nobody in.
Invest, since your relative has been paid on time every month for a year.
Start small and bring in a few friends so the bonuses cover your risk.

lens.name: Opportunity cost
lens.one_line: The true price of anything is the best thing you gave up to get it.
lens.detail: ₹5 lakh in a fixed deposit isn't 'safe' in isolation — its real cost is whatever that money would have done elsewhere, against inflation. Two hours commuting costs whatever those two hours were worth. This is also the honest way to evaluate any 'free' thing: free tends to be paid in time, attention or optionality.
elsewhere: A cheap flat 25 km out, priced in hours of your life per year.
Studying one more degree versus the earnings and experience forgone.
A free app paid for with attention and data.
lens.test: Not 'can I afford this?' but 'what is the best thing I'm giving up to have it?'
lens.today: The New Indian Express reports the new Pink Line stretch is saving time for South Bengaluru commuters, and Inshorts reports 33,409 riders on day one. The real cost of your current commute is not the fare, it is the hours a slower route takes from you every week. If the Pink Line touches your route, compare it in time saved per week, not only in rupees per trip.

moved.what: The Times of India reports the state government is moving to revise the guidance value for property, the second revision in three years, which may raise registration costs. It follows recent increases in milk and bus fares.
moved.so_what: If you are close to buying or registering a flat or site, ask your lawyer or builder this week what the current guidance value is and whether registering before the revision would save you money. Check the date it takes effect before you plan around it.

moved.what: Urban Acres reports white-topping work on Dr Rajkumar Road has brought a ban on heavy vehicles there.
moved.so_what: If your route uses Dr Rajkumar Road or the roads next to it, expect lorries and buses to be diverted onto nearby streets, and allow extra time until the work is done.

moved.what: The Hindu reports BMRCL has announced Pink Line timings while commuters are asking for faster completion of the underground section. The Federal reports first-day riders saw gaps as well as time savings.
moved.so_what: Check the published first and last train times before you rely on the Pink Line for a late return. The underground stretch is not open yet, so plan the rest of the trip by road for now.

moved.what: Deccan Herald reports CM DK Shivakumar says the government is planning door-to-door data collection across Bengaluru for residential records.
moved.so_what: When the survey starts, expect officials at your door. Ask for ID, give only what the survey needs, and never share an OTP, bank detail or payment, because fraudsters can copy a real government drive.

moved.what: The Times of India reports a Bengaluru woman lost ₹8 lakh in an Instagram gift scam.
moved.so_what: If a gift from an online contact needs you to pay a fee, customs charge or tax to release it, it is the scam. Stop paying and report it on 1930 or cybercrime.gov.in.

carry_over.prompt: At the counter, a ₹20 carry bag with the store's logo appears on your bill though nobody offered it; what is the tell?
carry_over.answer: A small charge that appears on the bill without being offered first is counting on you not checking.
